title: Forgotten forests
subtitle: Found only in the Deep South of the USA, longleaf pine woodlands have dwindled to about 3 percent of their former range, but new efforts are under way to restore them

paragraphs.text: The longleaf pine forest is among the richest ecosystems in North America, rivaling such wildlife habitats as the tallgrass prairies and the ancient forests of the Pacific Northwest in the number of species it shelters. And like those two other disappearing habitats, longleaf is also critically endangered.

Longleaf pines can grow to a height of 40 meters and live for 300 to 400 years. In longleaf pine forests, trees grow widely scattered, producing a sunny, open, park-like environment. This openness creates a forest floor that is among the most diverse in the world, home to a vast variety of animals and plants. As many as 50 different species of wildflowers, shrubs, grasses and ferns have been cataloged in just a single square meter of longleaf forest.

Once, nearly 92 million acres of longleaf forest flourished from Virginia to Texas. But by the turn of the 21st century virtually all of it had been logged, paved or farmed into oblivion. Only about 3 percent still survives, with an estimated 100,000 acres vanishing every year. However, a quiet movement to reverse this trend is rippling across the region. Governments, private organizations and individual conservationists are looking for ways to protect and preserve the remaining longleaf, and to plant new forests for future generations. This will also allow biologists to help the endangered plants and animals that depend on this habitat.

The demise of the longleaf forest's flora and fauna is also tied to a lack of fire, which once swept through the southern forests on a regular basis. ‘Fire is absolutely critical for this ecosystem and for the species that depend on it,’ says Mark Danaher, biologist for South Carolina's Francis Marion National Forest. The Bachman's sparrow is one such species. These small, secretive birds tuck their nests on the ground beneath clumps of wiregrass and little bluestem in the open understory. But once fire has been absent for several years, and a tangle of shrubs starts to grow, the sparrows disappear.

Name just about any species that occurs in longleaf and you can find a connection to fire. The gopher tortoise, a key species for these forests, digs burrows which provide homes and safety to more than 300 species of vertebrates and invertebrates, ranging from eastern diamondback rattlesnakes to gopher frogs. If fire is suppressed, however, the gopher tortoise is choked out.

Fire also knocks back the oaks and other hardwoods that can grow up to overwhelm longleaf forests. ‘They are fire forests,’ says Bob Mitchell, ecologist at the Jones Research Center, southwestern Georgia. ‘They evolved in the lightning capital of the eastern United States.’ And it wasn't only lightning strikes that set the forest aflame. ‘Native Americans also started fires to keep the forest open,’ Mitchell says. ‘So did European settlers. They helped create the longleaf pine forests that we know today.’

Fire also changes how nutrients flow throughout longleaf ecosystems. When Frances James, a bird expert from Florida State University, realized red-cockaded woodpeckers laid more eggs in the first breeding season after their territories were burned, she and her colleagues went searching for answers. ‘We learned calcium is stashed away in shrubs when the forest is not burned,’ James says. ‘But when there is a fire, pulses of calcium move from the shrubs into the soil and then up into the longleaf.’ Eventually, this calcium makes its way up the food chain to tree-dwelling ants, which are the woodpeckers' favorite food. The result: more calcium for the birds, which leads to more eggs, and more young woodpeckers.

Today, fire is used as a vital management tool for preserving both longleaf and its wildlife. By deliberately causing what they call ‘prescribed burns’, conservationists can reduce the risk of catastrophic conflagrations. ‘Forests are going to burn,’ says Amadou Diop, the National Wildlife Federation's (NWF) southern forests restoration manager. ‘It's just a question of when. With these low-intensity fires, we can pick the time and the place.’

Diop is spearheading a new NWF effort to restore longleaf. ‘It's a species we need to go back to,’ he says. Educating landowners about the advantages of growing longleaf is a key part of the program. ‘Right now, most existing longleaf is on public land,’ says Jerry McCollum, president of the Georgia Wildlife Federation. ‘Private land is where we need to work,’ he adds, pointing out that more than 90 percent of the area within the historic range of longleaf falls under this category.

Interest among private landowners is growing throughout the South, but restoring longleaf is not an easy task. It is not just a matter of growing the trees. The herbaceous layer — the understory of wiregrasses and other plants — also needs to be re-created. In areas where the land has not been chewed up by farming, but converted to plantations of other pine species, the seed bank of the longleaf forest usually remains viable beneath the soil. Where agriculture has destroyed the seeds, however, wiregrass must be replanted. Right now, the expense is prohibitive, but researchers are searching for low-cost solutions.

Bringing back longleaf is not for the short-sighted, however. Not many of us will be alive when the pines being planted today become mature forests in 70 to 80 years. But that is not stopping longleaf enthusiasts. ‘Today, it's getting hard to find longleaf seedlings to buy,’ says one Louisiana landowner. ‘Everyone wants them. Longleaf is in a resurgence.’
